claims.text: Structural and chemical stability across 473–1923 K is governed by temperature-dependent atomic diffusion kinetics.
At lower temperatures, high configurational entropy combined with slow atomic diffusion maintains a homogeneous solid solution.
At higher temperatures, accelerated atomic mobility leads to phase segregation and elemental clustering.
The initial material consists of nanoparticles containing at least five metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and crystallized as a single-phase solid solution.
The proposed intervention is incremental heating from 473 K to 1923 K under an inert or vacuum atmosphere.
An inert environment eliminates oxidative effects on the nanoparticles.
Atomic diffusion rate mediates the transition from entropy-associated retention of the solid solution to elemental segregation.
At lower temperatures, kinetic barriers to diffusion preserve the homogeneous solid solution.
Increasing temperature enhances atomic mobility sufficiently to produce chemical demixing.
Below a composition-dependent critical temperature, the nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous solid-solution phase.
Above the critical temperature, the nanoparticles will develop phase segregation and chemical inhomogeneity.
Phase segregation and chemical inhomogeneity will be detectable through changes in diffraction patterns and elemental-distribution maps.
Reactive atmospheres, external stresses, or substrate effects may shift the critical temperature or alter phase behavior.
The transition temperature depends on detailed alloy composition and experimental setup.
Peak splitting, peak broadening, or emergence of new XRD peaks can indicate structural phase changes.
Retention of a uniform single-phase solid solution throughout 473–1923 K, with no segregation or clustering, would falsify the hypothesis.
